newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to start securities reforms from 97/98--MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan to start securities reforms from 97/98--MOF.

text.p: The Finance Ministry said on Friday that Japan will implement the bulk of the securities deregulation steps recommended by a "Big Bang" reform panel within the current business year.

The deregulation steps are among proposals made on Friday by the Securities and Exchange Council, a panel advising the finance minister on liberalisation of the nation's securities markets under the government's financial Big Bang plans.
A Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said that 19 out of the 24 deregulation items linked to the securities industry and markets will be implemented in the 1997/98 business year.

Most of the five others will be carried out in the following financial year, 1998/99, he said, with the exception of steps related to stock-broking commissions and allowing the securities subsidiaries of banks to enter the stockbroking business.

He also said the proposals, which were unveiled earlier on Friday, stated that Japan must establish a framework to enable securities houses to create innovative financial products by abolishing various regulations.

The advisory panel also urged Japanese regulators to shift their focus to supervisory checks and away from using regulations as preventive measures, in order to create fair and reliable markets in Japan, he said.
To establish international markets in Japan that can compete with New York and London, it is not enough to merely copy financial products already offered in overseas markets, the council said.

To create fair and transparent markets, the council also proposed that harsher penalties be imposed for illegal stock transactions such as insider trading and stock manipulation, in line with global standards. It also called for stronger penalties for false statements by institutions to regulators.
The panel did not go into any detail on proposed stiffer penalties.

The council also called for inspection, market-monitoring and penalty systems to be strengthened at Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), in order to deal with complicated new financial products and services which may be offered.
